newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sudden U.S. Mir crew change surprises Russia.
newsitem.headline: Sudden U.S. Mir crew change surprises Russia.

text.p: Russian space officials said on Thursday they were surprised and confused by the sudden U.S. decision to replace the next astronaut scheduled to join the troubled Mir space station.
"For us it was very unexpected," said Valery Lyndin, a spokesman for Mission Control outside Moscow.

On Wednesday NASA astronaut Wendy Lawrence appeared at a news conference and expressed her eagerness to fly aboard Mir and replace Michael Foale in September. Then hours after putting her under the media spotlight, NASA officials announced her backup, David Wolf, would take her place aboard Mir.

U.S. officials said they made the decision because Lawrence, a Navy pilot, had no experience with spacewalks and did not fit into the Orlan Russian spacesuit. She will still fly on board the U.S. shuttle in mid-September.
The next Russian crew aboard Mir will attempt to make vital repairs to the space station, which crashed into a resupply ship on June 25 and is limping along on partial power.
Part of the repairs will require a spacewalk outside the punctured Spektr module, although the NASA astronaut is not expected to participate.

"Because of the number and nature of spacewalks and the nature of spacewalks under consideration by the Russians to repair the Spektr, we have discussed at length the advantage of having another astronaut qualified for these tasks," Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's cooperation with Mir, said in a statement on Thursday.
"As a result, the joint decision was made to have all three crew members on board qualified to handle spacewalking tasks."
But there appeared to be some some confusion in communications between U.S. and Russian space officials.
Boris Kryuchkov, deputy director of Russia's Star City cosmonaut training centre, said late on Thursday he had not received any information on a change of crew.
"Yes, we are working with them (the astronauts), but we have not received any such decision yet," he told Reuters. "We have no official documents, decisions, nothing has been decided."

He added that since Lawrence was not expected to make any spacewalks, she had never been fitted for a Russian space suit, which has the same size body for all, but adjustable arms and legs. Lyndin said smaller Russians had used such suits in the past.

"There were no objections to her from our side," Lyndin said, referring to Lawrence, who is 1.60 metres (five feet, three inches) tall. "We are only sorry she cannot fly, especially since she was so geared up to do such work."
Also on Thursday, Russian cosmonauts Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov left for the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan ahead of their scheduled August 5 blast off to Mir.

On August 20 they will try to reattach Spektr's interior cables, linked to solar panels outside, which should restore most power to the vessel. They are expected to perform their first spacewalk to inspect the Spektr's external puncture on September 3, and plan to do the repairs after that.

NASA said the September 20 launch of the U.S. shuttle carrying the next American astronaut may now be delayed to allow Wolf, a medical doctor also trained in electrical engineering, more time to complete spacewalk training at Star City.
Wolf had been scheduled to join Mir in January, and has already been training for several months at Star City, Kryuchkov said.
